name: Ben Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of seven on motor claims at Harbourline, a mid-sized car insurer with an office above the shopping arcade in town. Most of the day is bumps, scrapes and write-offs: I check the photos, read the garage estimate, call the customer and decide what we pay. The part I like is the phone calls, when someone's shaken after a crash and I can tell them their car is sorted. What wears me out is the targets board by the kitchen, with every handler's closed claims in red or green.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your life look like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a two-bedroom flat with my girlfriend Lucía, who's a nurse on nights at the general hospital, so we mostly swap notes on the fridge. I've got about three months of costs saved, which felt like a lot until the rent went up in spring. I'm also the union rep for our floor, which mostly means people bring me their problems at lunch. I don't use the AI stuff the company keeps pushing. I've never even clicked the button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, part of me would be relieved, because the managers have been talking about it like it's coming for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, told you so, it's a fancy autocomplete. At the union branch meeting I'd say the real fight was always pay and staffing, not robots. Online I wouldn't say much, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the routine bits would still get chipped off. The first-notice-of-loss forms, the letters, the chasing emails. That's maybe a third of what my newer handlers do, so even a small change means management asks why we need seven people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and keep my head down on the software. I'd push at the union branch for a staffing agreement, so any time saved goes into handling calls properly, not cutting a desk. And I'd keep topping up the savings by a bit each month, because the rent isn't going back down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit tired of the whole argument. It's not AI I lose sleep over in that world, it's the rent and the targets board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's the rent and the targets board. Which of those weighs more right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent. We went up by nearly a tenth in April and Lucía's pay didn't move. If Harbourline froze bonuses again like two years ago, we'd be eating into savings by summer. The targets board just makes me grumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about, even in this calmer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemi, who joined last year straight from college. She does a lot of the first-notice forms, the boring intake stuff, and that's exactly what a bit of automation would eat. She's sharp, but she's the newest, and newest goes first.

say: I'd tell colleagues AI was a **fancy autocomplete** all along.
I'd tell the union branch the real fight was always **pay and staffing**.
think: I think the **routine forms and letters** would still get chipped away.
That's about **a third** of my newer handlers' work, so a desk could go.
do: Keep handling claims the way I do and **avoid the software**.
Push at the union branch for a **staffing agreement** on saved time.
Top up **savings** a little each month to cover the higher rent.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but tired of hearing about AI at work.
The **rent** worries me more than any machine does.
S0.quote: It's not AI I lose sleep over in that world, it's the rent and the targets board.
fieldNote: His real pressure in this world is **rent**, which rose nearly a tenth in April.
He sees **junior intake work** as the first thing even small automation would take.
Union role gives him a **ready answer**: fight for staffing, not against tools.

steps.text: Carry on leading the motor claims team without the AI button
Propose a staffing agreement at the next union branch meeting
Put a little extra into savings each month against the rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Writing, checking and answering customers. That's my whole job description, pretty much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need it in writing, through the union, that nobody loses their job to software without a proper process. I'd tell friends the companies get the savings and we get the stress. If I posted, it'd be to share the union's campaign, not my own opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Harbourline would stop replacing people. Not sack them, just not hire when someone leaves, and give the rest a target that assumes the software does half the work. I'm the best handler on the floor, but I'm also the one who won't touch the tool. That combination doesn't end well for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to ask for a written agreement on hiring and redeployment. I'd cut back, no holiday this year, cancel the streaming and the gym. I'd start looking at the other two insurers in town, though they'd have the same software. I'd probably have to learn the tool eventually, but I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, honestly. Like I'm standing on the platform and everyone else got on the train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on learning the tool. Why, when it might keep you in a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I learn their system, they use it to measure me harder. I learned the last claims platform and they put the targets board up a month later. Maybe that's stubborn. My manager Priya says it's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucía the night you heard the first desk wasn't being replaced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucía we're fine for now, and I'd mean the for now part. She'd tell me to stop being proud and learn the thing. Nurses don't have much patience for people who won't adapt, she sees too much of it.

say: I'd demand a **written agreement** that software never costs a job without process.
I'd tell friends companies keep the **savings** and staff get the stress.
think: I expect Harbourline to **stop replacing** people who leave.
Being the best handler who **refuses the tool** leaves me exposed.
do: Ask the union to negotiate **hiring and redeployment** terms in writing.
Cancel the **holiday, streaming and gym** this year.
Look at the **two other insurers** in town, though they'd use the same software.
feel: **Left behind**, like everyone else already got on the train.
S1.quote: I'm the best handler on the floor, but I'm also the one who won't touch the tool. That combination doesn't end well for me.
fieldNote: He links learning new systems to **harsher targets**, which explains his resistance.
He openly admits **refusing the tool** makes him vulnerable, yet holds the line.
Lucía, a nurse, is the **voice pushing** him to adapt.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate written hiring and redeployment terms
Cancel this year's holiday, streaming and gym membership
Apply to the two other insurers in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not a change in how I work, that's the end of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. At the branch, online, everywhere. I'd say the government needs to slow it down, tax the companies using it, and pay people properly while they retrain. I'd go to whatever march the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job by 2028. Motor claims is photos, estimates and letters. A machine that can do any thinking work does that in seconds, and my bosses would switch it on the same week. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because there's nothing hands-on in what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut spending hard and move every spare bit into savings. I'd talk to my uncle Rafa, who has a small tiling business, about learning the trade, because hands-on work gets roughly three more years. I'd stay in the union fight the whole time. And Lucía and I would probably look for a cheaper flat, or move in with her sister for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums on my phone while Lucía's at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those sums look like, at three in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of savings, half the rent if Lucía carries more, and her nurse's pay. Hospitals still need nurses with hands. So maybe a year if we're careful, before I'm asking my mum for help. I hate even saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn tiling, but robots come for that too around 2031. Is that worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is three years. Rafa says you learn the basics in six months and you're useful in a year. It buys time while the politics catches up, if it ever does. I'm not under any illusion it's a forever job.

say: I'd call loudly for government to **slow it down** and tax the companies.
I'd join any **union march** and push for paid retraining.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2028.
Robots coming later **doesn't help** because my work has nothing hands-on.
do: Cut spending hard and **save every spare bit** from now.
Learn **tiling** with my uncle Rafa for roughly three extra years.
Move to a **cheaper flat** or in with Lucía's sister.
feel: **Sick**, doing money sums awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Rafa (his uncle) says you learn tiling in six months. Three years is three years.
fieldNote: He sees a straight line from **full AGI** to the end of motor claims work.
Hands-on **tiling** is his bridge, chosen for the three-year robot gap.
Nurse partner's income is the household's **main anchor** in this world.
He'd sooner ask **family** than the state, but expects to need both.

steps.text: Join every union march and campaign for paid retraining
Start learning tiling with uncle Rafa on Saturdays
Move to a cheaper flat or in with Lucía's sister
Lean on Lucía's nurse pay and family if savings run out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast. But at least you'd see the trucks coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, louder and earlier. We've got five years, so let's use them to get laws in place, not just watch. I'd push the union to get a redundancy deal agreed before anything's switched on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it buys me time in the job, not a future in it. By 2031 the thinking work's gone, and by 2034 the hands-on stuff too. I'd have to decide early, and deciding early is the thing I'm worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time electrician course at the college in year one, because Lucía keeps saying they're short. I'd keep the Harbourline job and the union role while I train. I'd save hard, and I'd vote for whoever promised a proper transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less panic than the two-year one, but more dread, because I'd have to watch it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said deciding early is what you're worst at. What would make you actually sign up for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Lucía filling in the form and leaving it on the fridge. That's how I ended up at the dentist last year. Joking aside, a redundancy announcement would do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, my manager, oddly. She's 50, she's all spreadsheets, and she's spent twenty years at Harbourline. She'd be gone the same year as me, with a lot less time to start over.

say: I'd push to **get laws in place** while there are five years.
I'd want the union to win a **redundancy deal** before anything's switched on.
think: Five years buys **time in the job**, not a future in it.
I'd have to **decide early**, which I find hardest.
do: Start a part-time **electrician course** at the college in year one.
Keep the job and **union role** while training.
Vote for whoever offers a **transition fund**.
feel: **Dread** rather than panic, from watching it come.
S3.quote: Five years buys me time in the job, not a future in it.
fieldNote: He knows he **decides late** and expects an external push, like a redundancy notice.
He chooses an **electrician course** because his partner says the trade is short.
He worries for his **older manager** Priya more than himself.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time electrician course at the college
Push the union for a redundancy deal before the switch-on
Vote for candidates who back a transition fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That one I can at least think about without my stomach dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when to plan, with the union and the government at the table. Ten years is enough to retrain a generation if somebody bothers to organise it. I'd be pushing for that at every branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's still my job going. I'd be 37 in 2036, which is a terrible age to start over but not an impossible one. And my own resistance is the real risk, because ten years makes it easy to keep saying next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline: electrician apprenticeship started by 30, while I'm still at Harbourline part time if they'd let me. I'd build savings up to six months. I'd keep the union work going. Lucía and I would hold off buying anywhere until I knew what I'd earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. More like knowing the boiler will break one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off buying a place. How long have you two been planning that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Since we moved in together, four years now. Lucía wants a garden. I'd tell her we wait three more years while I sort the trade. She'd be annoyed, but she'd get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years makes it easy to say next year, you said. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing it down with a date, and telling Rafa and Lucía so they nag me. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid. Being embarrassed in front of family works on me better than any manager.

say: I'd say ten years is **exactly when to plan** with union and government.
I'd push to **retrain a generation** at every branch meeting.
think: My job **still goes**, just later, when I'd be 37.
My own **stubbornness** is the biggest risk with so much time.
do: Build **savings** to six months of costs.
Hold off **buying a home** with Lucía until earnings are clear.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing the boiler will break one day.
S4.quote: I'd be 37 in 2036, which is a terrible age to start over but not an impossible one.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his panic into **a plan with a date**.
He uses **family pressure** to beat his own habit of delay.
Home-buying with Lucía is the **family plan** that pays the price.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship before turning 30
Build savings up to six months of household costs
Delay buying a house with Lucía for three years
Keep pushing for retraining plans at union branch meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. I'd have a nurse's pay, three months of savings and a trade I haven't learned yet. What would help is the government paying people a proper wage while they retrain, not a leaflet and a website. And a law that makes companies give real notice before switching a team off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people why they won't use these tools, not just whether. For me it's not fear of the tech. Every system they gave us became a way to watch us closer. If the tools came with a promise that the time saved was ours, I might even click the button.

headlineQuote: Every system they gave us became a way to watch us closer.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old team lead** on motor claims, renting with his nurse girlfriend Lucía.
He's the best handler on his floor but **refuses the AI tools**, tying them to harsher targets.
As **union rep**, he answers every scenario with collective bargaining and calls for regulation.
Faster AGI pushes him from union fights towards **learning a trade**, tiling or electrical work.
His mood climbs from uneasy about **rent** to alarmed when AGI arrives within five years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only three months of savings and no trade learned yet.
whatWouldHelp: A **proper wage while retraining**, paid by government, not just advice.
A law forcing **real notice** before companies switch a team off.
